synopsis: Building off-road virtual validation requires simultaneous specialist coverage across simulation architecture, machine and soil dynamics, sensor modeling, 3D assets, test automation, data and cloud infrastructure, ECU/HIL, statistics, and safety; the corpus identifies these disciplines but finds no defensible mapping to a specific headcount [f8773, f8774]. No independent 2024–2026 benchmark establishes cost, staffing or time to first useful result from zero; the on-road PEGASUS precedent involved 17 partners, about 1,791 person-months and EUR 34.5 million, rather than establishing a single manufacturer's staffing prescription [f8734, f1287, f1544, f1575]. Engineering labor dominates compute costs, with an estimated floor of USD 150,000–260,000 per specialist annually, so even free software can yield a seven-figure annual programme [f16234, f8318]. With no internal capability and nine months before hardware, the booklet favors hybrid implementation, while partner-led work still needs an internal core owning requirements and acceptance [f16138, f8765]. Governance should establish an accountable technical owner, explicit ownership of tool qualification and model credibility, and independent review; the organization currently lacks documented credibility foundations, and on-road EU requirements explicitly demand competence evidence for both toolchain validators and users [f10265, f5792, f8049, f10414, f10596]. Planning must quantify scarce engineering capacity and address sustainment after September 2027, which remains a blind spot [f10273, f10367].
